latin.195:
ANNOTATIO III.
De Moliminibus pro Consociatione susceptis, ad pag. 334. ad 341.
§. I.
Simulac Dissensus initium subortum fuisset, in ipsa herba suffocare illud annisus est nullis satis laudibus evehendus Landgravius Hassiae Philippus,
latin.196: pluribus eam in rem ad Lutherum, Melanchtonem & Brentium datis literis, Concordiam, tàm ante Augustana Comitia, quàm in ipsis celebratis, & fraternitatem cum Zvinglianis ineundam servandamq; seriò suadentibus, quae exstant apud Chytraeum in Actis cum Zwinglianis, indignantibus quoq;, dictos Theologos, Consensum fidei fundamentalem Zwinglianorum secum, haud agnoscere velle.
latin.197: Sic enim Illustrissimus Princeps pro Zwinglianis in quadam Epistola disputat: Itaque mihi videtur, cùm in aliis Articulis vobiscum consentiant Zwingliani & Christum eâdem ratione, quâ vos, confiteantur, concedant etiam Christum in Coena per fidem manducari, quae Manducatio ad Salutem necessaria est, nec Omnipotentiae laudem Deo adimant, sed juxta Analogiam fidei Secundum Scripturam, sic intelligenda esse verba sentiant, ut ipsi intelligunt: Cùmq;, Christus, quia clarificatum Corpus habet, quô venter cibari nequit, vix aliter manducari possit, quàm à credentibus & per fidem; hac, inquam, cum ita se habeant, mihi videtur Sententia & Responsio vestra durior & non necessaria esse, spero etiam, Deo dante, vos diligentiùs cogitaturos & veriorem Sententiam secuturos esse, Chytraeus. Hist. August. Confess. p. 652. Responsorias Lutheri vide in Supplemento Buddeano nupero, Epistola 122. pag. 1024. 102.
latin.198: Quibus omnibus Landgravius tandem effecit, ut Marpurgum ad se excurrerent Theologi utriusque partis, seque praesente, anno 1529. Consensum Universalem, uno excepto de Coena Domini Articulo, inirent.
latin.199: Qua de re ita Chytraeus: Zwinglius & Oecolampadius libenter, in caeteris omnibus, Lutheri Sententiam secuti sunt, de Sacramento tantùm sequi noluerunt p. 643. Etsi autem, an verum Corpus & Sanguis Christi Corporaliter in Pane & Vino Coenae Domini praesens sit, hoc tempore non concordavimus, tamen una pars alteri Christianam dilectionem, quantum cujusq; Conscientia feret, declarabit, & utraque pars Deum Omnipotentem diligenter orabit, ut nos Spiritu suo in vera Sententia confirmet, pag. 646. Addit Clariss. Buddeus, Prof. Hallensis celeberrimus, in Supplemento, Epistolam Lutheri 98. Joh. Agricolae inscriptam suasoriam quò omnia aspera verba & Scripta cessarent in posterum pag. 71. 72. Ipse praetereà Chytraeus contestatur initio Hist. suae de Actis cum Zwingl. secum omnibus piis optare, quò dissidiorum odiorumq; acerbitas leniatur & mitigetur. pag. 636.
latin.200: MARPURGENSE hoc, Primum perfectiorum Consociationis moliminum dixerim, etsi Gradûs infimi: Perfectiorum, quia Consensus fuit ratione omnium dogmatum, exceptô unô; At Infimi Gradus, quia dextram Fraternitatis Lutherus dare noluit Chyt. pag. 647.
latin.201: Quin Haereticos Zwinglianos appellavit, in Epistola 103. Buddei Supplementi pag. 105. scribens Jacobo Probstio Theologiae Licentiato, his inter cetera, verbis: Indignissimè affecti sunt Zwingliani, quod Fratrum nomen non potuerunt obtinere, sed pro haereticis discedere cogerentur, tamen sic, ut pacem interim haberemus mutuis scriptis, si fortè Deus illis aperuerit Cor. Hôc pacto Schismatis Protestantici primus Autor, Lutherus; tantò intempestivè magis, quantò studiosius altera pars concordiam quaesivit, ipso fatente Luthero, Epist. 98. & 123. apud Buddeum, quando scribit: Zwinglium palam lacrymantem coram Landgravio & Ordinibus rogasse inque haec verba erupisse: Es seynd keine Leut auff Erden / mit denen ich lieber wolte Eines seyn / dann mit den Wittenbergern pag. 105. Iterumque: Zwinglianos promisisse, se velle cum Lutheranis dicere, Christi Corpus veraciter esse in Coena praesens, sed spiritualiter tantum, ut eos fratres dignaremur appellare. Ibidem.

pass_a.195: ANNOTATIO III. On the Efforts undertaken for Consociation, at pages 334 to 341. §. I. As soon as the Dissensus had first sprung up, the Landgrave of Hesse Philip — who cannot be praised enough — tried to smother that thing in the very blade of grass,
pass_a.196: with many letters given on that matter to Luther, Melanchthon, and Brentius, seriously urging Concord — both before the Augsburg Diet and in the Diet itself once convened — and fraternity to be entered into and kept with the Zwinglians, which letters stand in Chytraeus in the Acts with the Zwinglians, the said Theologians also being indignant and unwilling to acknowledge a fundamental consensus of faith of the Zwinglians with themselves.
pass_a.197: For thus the Most Illustrious Prince argues for the Zwinglians in a certain Epistle: Therefore it seems to me, since in the other Articles the Zwinglians agree with you and confess Christ in the same way you do, and also concede that Christ is eaten in the Supper by faith — which Eating is necessary to Salvation — and do not take from God the praise of Omnipotence, but hold the words to be understood according to the Analogy of faith according to Scripture as they themselves understand: and since Christ, because He has a glorified Body which the belly cannot be fed with, can scarcely be eaten otherwise than by believers and through faith; these things, I say, being so, your Sentence and Response seem to me harder and not necessary, and I hope also, God granting, that you will think more carefully and follow a truer Sentence — Chytraeus, History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 652. See Luther’s replies in the recent Buddean Supplement, Epistle 122, pages 1024, 102.
pass_a.198: By all which the Landgrave at last brought it about that the Theologians of both parties should travel out to him at Marburg, and, he being present, in the year 1529 enter into a Universal Consensus, with one Article excepted — that on the Lord’s Supper.
pass_a.199: On which matter Chytraeus thus: Zwingli and Oecolampadius willingly followed Luther’s Sentence in all the rest; on the Sacrament alone they refused to follow, p. 643. Although, however, whether the true Body and Blood of Christ be Corporally present in the Bread and Wine of the Lord’s Supper we have not agreed at this time, yet one party will declare Christian love to the other as far as each one’s Conscience will bear, and both parties will diligently pray God Almighty that He confirm us by His Spirit in the true Sentence, p. 646. The most distinguished Buddeus, the celebrated Halle Professor, adds in the Supplement Luther’s Epistle 98 addressed to Johann Agricola, persuasive that thereafter all harsh words and Writings should cease, pp. 71–72. Chytraeus himself moreover testifies at the start of his History of the Acts with the Zwinglians that he with all the pious wishes the bitterness of dissensions and hatreds be softened and mitigated, p. 636.
pass_a.200: This MARBURG one I would call the First of the more perfect Consociation efforts, though of the lowest Grade: more perfect, because the Consensus was with respect to all dogmas, one excepted; but of the lowest Grade, because Luther refused to give the right hand of Fraternity — Chytraeus p. 647.
pass_a.201: Indeed he called the Zwinglians Heretics, in Epistle 103 of Buddeus’s Supplement p. 105, writing to Jakob Probst, Licentiate of Theology, among other words: The Zwinglians were most unworthily treated, in that they could not obtain the name of Brothers, but were compelled to depart as heretics, yet so that we might meanwhile have peace by mutual writings, if perhaps God should open their Heart. By this pact Luther was the first Author of the Protestant Schism — all the more untimely, the more studiously the other party sought Concord, Luther himself confessing it, Epistles 98 and 123 in Buddeus, when he writes that Zwingli, openly weeping before the Landgrave and the Estates, begged and broke out into these words: There are no people on earth with whom I would rather be one than with the Wittenbergers, p. 105. And again: that the Zwinglians had promised they were willing to say with the Lutherans that Christ’s Body is truly present in the Supper, but only spiritually, so that we might deign to call them brothers. Ibidem.

195: ANNOTATIO III. On the Attempts Made toward Consociation (pages 334–341).
§. I. The moment the Dissensus first broke out, Landgrave Philip of Hesse — a prince hard to praise enough — tried to choke it off in the bud.
196: He wrote again and again to Luther, Melanchthon, and Brentius, pressing hard for Concord — both before the Augsburg Diet and while it sat — and for fraternity with the Zwinglians that would actually be kept.

Those letters are still in Chytraeus’s Acts with the Zwinglians; and the named theologians, for their part, were angry and would not admit that the Zwinglians shared with them a fundamental consensus of faith.
197: So the Most Illustrious Prince argues for the Zwinglians in one letter (Chytraeus, History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 652): since they agree with you in the other articles, confess Christ as you do, grant that Christ is eaten in the Supper by faith — and that eating is needed for salvation — and do not strip God of omnipotence, but read the words by the analogy of faith according to Scripture as they take them; and since Christ’s glorified body cannot feed a stomach, so He can scarcely be eaten except by believers and through faith — your sentence and reply look harder than they need to be, and I hope God will bring you to a truer view.
For Luther’s answering letters, see the recent Buddeus Supplement, Epistle 122, pages 1024 and 102.
198: By all of this the Landgrave at last got the theologians of both sides to come out to him at Marburg, and there in 1529, with him present, they entered a Universal Consensus — one article excepted: the Lord’s Supper.
199: On that outcome Chytraeus writes: Zwingli and Oecolampadius gladly followed Luther’s teaching in everything else; only on the Sacrament they would not follow (p. 643).

Though they had not yet agreed whether Christ’s true body and blood are corporally present in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, each side would still show the other Christian love as far as conscience allowed, and both would pray God to confirm them by His Spirit in the true teaching (p. 646).
Buddeus, the noted Halle professor, adds in his Supplement Luther’s Epistle 98 to Johann Agricola, urging that harsh words and writings stop from then on (pp. 71–72).
Chytraeus himself, opening his History of the Acts with the Zwinglians, says he and all the pious wish the bitterness of these splits and hatreds softened and eased (p. 636).
200: I would call this Marburg attempt the first of the more complete Consociation efforts — though still of the lowest grade.
More complete, because they agreed on every dogma but one; lowest grade, because Luther would not give the right hand of fraternity (Chytraeus, p. 647).
201: Worse: Luther called the Zwinglians heretics — Epistle 103 in Buddeus’s Supplement, p. 105, to Jakob Probst, Licentiate of Theology: they were treated most unfairly in being denied the name of brothers and forced to leave as heretics, yet so that peace might hold for a time by mutual writings, if God should open their heart.

On that footing Luther became the first author of the Protestant schism — and the more out of season, the more carefully the other side had sought Concord, as Luther himself admits in Epistles 98 and 123 in Buddeus.
He records that Zwingli, weeping openly before the Landgrave and the Estates, begged and cried out: there are no people on earth with whom I would rather be one than with the Wittenbergers (p. 105).
And again: the Zwinglians had promised they would say with the Lutherans that Christ’s body is truly present in the Supper, but only spiritually — if only they might be called brothers. Same place.
